ideas.hypothesis: Financial sector reform changes the direction of finance-growth causality: before liberalization causality runs from GDP growth to financial deepening (demand-following), while after reform it runs from financial deepening to growth (supply-leading), so full-sample tests hide a regime shift.

sources.role: setting and finding: Uganda 1970-2002, positive finance-growth link and a significant financial-reform dummy after the 1992 reforms
method: Granger-causality tests of which variable leads in transition economies

ideas.test: Annual Uganda data 1970-2019 (WDI/IFS: private credit/GDP, M2/GDP, real GDP per capita). Estimate VAR/VECM Granger-causality tests separately for 1970-1991 and 1992-2019, plus rolling-window or time-varying causality tests. Replicate on 5-10 sub-Saharan African countries with documented reform dates.
ideas.disconfirming: Causality runs the same way (or is absent) in both sub-periods, or the rolling tests show no change in direction around the reform dates.

ideas.hypothesis: The positive population-growth effect reported for Pakistan comes from growth in the working-age share. Once the change in the working-age-to-total-population ratio is controlled for, total population growth has a zero or negative effect on GDP per capita growth.

sources.role: finding and setting: simple regression showing a positive population-growth effect on Pakistan's growth
method: decomposing growth into contribution ratios of individual factors

ideas.test: Pakistan 1960-2019 annual data from WDI and UN World Population Prospects: GDP growth, GDP per capita growth, population growth and working-age share growth. Run ARDL/cointegration regressions of per capita growth on population growth, with and without working-age share growth. Extend to a South Asian country panel.
ideas.disconfirming: Population growth keeps a significant positive coefficient on per capita growth after the change in working-age share is controlled for.

ideas.hypothesis: Causality runs in different directions for different spending components: GDP growth Granger-causes 'maintaining' (administrative) expenditure, as Wagner's law predicts, while social expenditure Granger-causes GDP growth. Mixing the two explains the insignificant or negative aggregate spending-growth estimates.

sources.role: measure and finding: social, economic and maintaining expenditures have different signs and significance for growth, 1980-2004
mechanism: growth and fiscal (tax) growth affect each other and move together in the long run

ideas.test: Chinese provincial panel 1995-2019 of spending by functional category (China Statistical Yearbooks / Finance Yearbooks) plus provincial GDP. Run Dumitrescu-Hurlin panel Granger-causality tests for each component and for total spending.
ideas.disconfirming: Growth does not Granger-cause maintaining spending, social spending does not lead growth, or causality runs the same way for every component.

ideas.hypothesis: Per yuan of fiscal cost, R&D tax incentives raise provincial output and TFP growth more than direct R&D subsidies do. The gap widens with existing enterprise R&D intensity, because tax incentives complement market R&D.

sources.role: mechanism and finding: a calibrated growth model in which tax incentives complement market R&D and have the larger growth effect
mechanism: the R&D-driven endogenous growth models behind the R&D-growth link

ideas.test: Chinese provincial panel 2007-2019 with government R&D funds given to enterprises (subsidy) and R&D super-deduction/high-tech tax relief (incentive), from the China Statistical Yearbook on Science and Technology. Regress GDP or TFP growth on both instruments, scaled by fiscal cost and interacted with lagged enterprise R&D intensity. Use the national changes in super-deduction rates as shocks.
ideas.disconfirming: Subsidies have an equal or larger growth effect per yuan, or the advantage of tax incentives does not rise with private R&D intensity.

ideas.hypothesis: Fourth-quarter macro growth predicts bond returns because of year-end consumer confidence. The Q4 change in consumer confidence predicts next-year excess bond returns and absorbs most of the predictive power of Q4 GDP growth.

sources.role: finding and method: Q4 growth predicts stock and bond returns, works in-sample and out-of-sample, and is linked to growth in consumer confidence

ideas.test: US data 1960-2019: Michigan sentiment and Conference Board confidence indices, quarterly real GDP/consumption growth, excess Treasury bond returns (CRSP). Run predictive regressions of annual excess bond returns on the Q4 confidence change versus Q1-Q3 changes, with and without Q4 GDP growth, and check out-of-sample R-squared.
ideas.disconfirming: The Q4 confidence change does not predict bond returns, or the predictive coefficient on Q4 GDP growth is unchanged once confidence is added.

ideas.hypothesis: More generous pay-as-you-go pensions lower fertility. The effect is stronger where bequests are mostly accidental (lower adult survival, small intentional transfers) than where intentional bequest motives are strong, as an endogenous-growth model with bequest motives implies.

sources.role: mechanism and testable implications: bequest motives change how PAYG Social Security affects fertility, saving and growth, and accidental-bequest outcomes depend on survival probability

ideas.test: Panel of about 35 OECD and Latin American countries 1970-2015: PAYG contribution and replacement rates (OECD Pensions at a Glance; Social Security Programs Throughout the World), total fertility rate, adult survival probability, and inheritance flows/GDP where available. Fixed-effects regressions of fertility on pension generosity interacted with survival and bequest-flow measures.
ideas.disconfirming: Pension generosity is unrelated to fertility, or its effect does not differ with survival or bequest prevalence.

ideas.hypothesis: In transition economies, growth in imports of capital and intermediate goods Granger-causes GDP growth while growth in consumer-goods imports does not. This sharpens the finding that growth in these economies is shaped by import demand.

sources.role: setting, method and finding: causality tests in 13 transition economies show growth-led exports and growth shaped by import demand
mechanism: moving from a 'barring' to an 'introducing' growth pattern by importing advanced technology and joining the international division of labor

ideas.test: 13 transition economies 1995-2019, annual or quarterly. Split imports by Broad Economic Categories using UN Comtrade and combine with real GDP. Run panel VAR Granger-causality tests separately for capital/intermediate and consumer imports.
ideas.disconfirming: Capital and intermediate imports do not Granger-cause growth, or consumer imports show the same causality.

ideas.hypothesis: Conditional convergence is faster among countries with more economic freedom: in growth regressions, the interaction between initial log GDP per capita and an economic freedom index is negative.

sources.role: finding: economic freedom is significantly related to growth across countries, beyond macroeconomic determinants
measure: a relative-growth (S-shaped) measure that separates growth, development and underdevelopment for convergence analysis
mechanism: institutions treated as an endogenous growth variable

ideas.test: About 120 countries 1980-2019 using Penn World Table and the Fraser Economic Freedom of the World index. Barro-type regressions over 5-year periods, estimated by system GMM, with an initial income x freedom interaction.
ideas.disconfirming: The interaction coefficient is zero or positive, so convergence is no faster in freer economies.

ideas.hypothesis: Spillovers from a nodal growth pole to its hinterland weaken with road travel time. Districts within a threshold travel time grow faster, more distant districts suffer backwash, and road upgrades push the threshold outward.

sources.role: setting and mechanism: spillover effects of the Mamminasata nodal centre on hinterland labor and enterprise development in South Sulawesi
mechanism: infrastructure as a driver of growth and competitiveness

ideas.test: Indonesian district (kabupaten/kota) GDP 2000-2019 from BPS, for South Sulawesi and several other provinces, plus road-network travel times to the provincial capital before and after major road upgrades. Regress district growth on travel time and its square, interacted with upgrade timing.
ideas.disconfirming: Hinterland growth shows no decline with travel time, or road upgrades leave the gradient unchanged.

ideas.hypothesis: Internet diffusion raises the TFP (Solow residual) contribution to regional growth with a 3-5 year lag, after a short initial dip in measured TFP (a productivity J-curve).

sources.role: mechanism: the internet and IT as drivers of the 'new economy' and of growth
method: growth accounting with factor contribution ratios

ideas.test: Chinese provincial panel 2000-2019. Compute Solow residuals by growth accounting (perpetual-inventory capital, labor, human capital) and take internet and broadband penetration from CNNIC. Run distributed-lag fixed-effects regressions of TFP growth on lagged penetration.
ideas.disconfirming: There is no positive lagged association between internet penetration and TFP growth, or only a contemporaneous association consistent with reverse causality.
